title: What psychology is
description: Psychology, named from Greek words for "soul" and "study of", is today the scientific study of the mind and behavior.

facts.text: The word psychology comes from Greek psykhe, meaning "breath, spirit, soul", plus -logia, meaning "study of".
Psychology is the scientific study of the mind and behavior.

title: Measuring a mind you cannot see
description: Because no one can read minds directly, psychologists test ideas by measuring things they can observe (behavior, biological signals and what people report) and publishing results so others can repeat them.

facts.text: Scientists test only what can be perceived and measured: the idea that a bird sings because it is happy cannot be tested, since there is no way to measure a bird's happiness, but people can be asked why they sing.

Because no one can read another person's mind, psychologists study mental processes indirectly by measuring observable behavior, biological indicators and self-reports, and draw inferences about the mind from them.
Psychologists test a hypothesis by observation or experiment and then publish or present the results so that others can replicate or build on them.

title: The main areas of psychology
description: Psychology splits into areas such as biopsychology, cognitive, developmental, social and personality psychology, organized in the APA into 54 divisions.

facts.text: Biopsychology studies how the nervous system relates to behavior, and cognitive psychology studies thoughts and how they relate to experience and action.

Developmental psychology studies change across the lifespan, social psychology studies how people interact with and relate to others, and personality psychology studies the patterns of thought and behavior that make each person unique.
The American Psychological Association (APA), the largest organization of psychologists in the world, has 54 divisions representing specialties within psychology.

title: Psychologists, psychiatrists and counselors
description: Psychologists hold a doctorate and assess and treat with therapy and testing; psychiatrists are medical doctors who can prescribe; counselors and therapists usually hold a master's degree.

facts.text: Clinical psychology receives the most attention in popular media, and many people mistakenly assume that all psychology is clinical psychology.
In the United States, psychologists who treat people hold a doctoral degree (a PhD or a PsyD); they assess people with interviews and psychological tests, make diagnoses and provide therapy.
Psychiatrists are medical doctors (MD or DO) who have completed training in psychiatry; because of that medical training they can prescribe medication, and they can also diagnose and provide therapy.
Counselors and therapists usually hold a master's degree in a mental health field and are licensed under titles such as Licensed Professional Counselor.
Only people who pass a licensure exam, after meeting state requirements, can call themselves licensed clinical or counseling psychologists.

title: Where psychologists work
description: Psychologists work in clinical and counseling practice, schools, courts, workplaces and university research.

facts.text: Clinical psychology focuses on diagnosing and treating psychological disorders, while counseling psychology focuses on emotional, social, vocational and health outcomes in people considered psychologically healthy.
Forensic psychologists work within the justice system, for example assessing whether a person is competent to stand trial and advising on eyewitness testimony.
Industrial-organizational psychologists apply psychology in workplaces, school psychologists work in education, and many psychologists with a PhD teach and do research at universities.

title: Wundt's first psychology laboratory
description: In 1879 Wilhelm Wundt opened the first psychology laboratory, at Leipzig, bringing experiments and measurement such as reaction times to questions that had belonged to philosophy.

facts.text: Wilhelm Wundt, a German scientist with a medical degree who taught physiology, established the first psychology laboratory at the University of Leipzig in 1879.
Until Wundt, psychology had been regarded as a branch of philosophy; he stressed experimental methods drawn from the natural sciences.
In Wundt's laboratory, a participant received a stimulus such as a light, image or sound and pressed a button, and an apparatus recorded the reaction time to one-thousandth of a second.

title: Introspection
description: Wundt used trained introspection, people examining their own conscious experience, but reports stayed subjective and observers often disagreed.

facts.text: Wundt used introspection, in which a trained person examines their own conscious experience as objectively as possible, aiming to find the components of consciousness.
Despite training, introspection remained highly subjective, and there was very little agreement between individuals.

title: Freud's unconscious mind
description: Sigmund Freud, a medical doctor, pictured most of the mind as an unconscious store of hidden feelings and urges, reached through dreams, free association and slips of the tongue.

facts.text: Sigmund Freud was an Austrian neurologist, a medical doctor rather than a psychologist.
Freud compared the mind to an iceberg, saying that only about one-tenth of it is conscious and the rest is unconscious.

Freud saw the unconscious mind as a store of feelings and urges we are not aware of, which he believed could be reached through dream analysis, the first words that come to mind and slips of the tongue.
Psychoanalysis, in which a patient talks about their experiences, was popularized by Freud and is still used today.

title: What Freud got wrong and right
description: Freud treated his own interpretations as proof, and most of his specific ideas, like his childhood stages, found no research support, while the broad idea that much of mental life is unconscious did.

facts.text: Freud treated his own recollections and his interpretations of patients' experiences and dreams as sufficient proof that his stages of childhood development were universal.
Most of Freud's specific ideas, such as his stages of childhood development, have not found support in modern research.

In a 1998 review, the psychologist Drew Westen found that a large body of research supports Freud's broad ideas that much of mental life is unconscious and that childhood experience helps shape personality.

title: Behaviorism
description: John Watson's behaviorism (1913) set aside introspection and the mind to study only observable behavior, aiming to predict and control it, and dominated American psychology for decades.

facts.text: In a 1913 paper, John B. Watson wrote that psychology as the behaviorist views it is a purely objective, experimental branch of natural science whose goal is the prediction and control of behavior, and that introspection forms no essential part of its methods.
Watson believed objective analysis of the mind was impossible, so he focused directly on observable behavior; this approach became known as behaviorism.
Behaviorism dominated experimental psychology for several decades; especially in North America, it dominated through the 1950s.
Behaviorism's objective methods, especially experiments, helped establish psychology as a science, and its ideas are still used in behavioral therapy and classrooms.

title: Skinner and consequences
description: B. F. Skinner studied how consequences (reinforcement and punishment) change behavior, often using animals in a chamber of his design.

facts.text: B. F. Skinner, like Watson a behaviorist, concentrated on how behavior is affected by its consequences, treating reinforcement and punishment as major drivers of behavior.
Behaviorists commonly experimented on animals, such as rats in a Skinner box, assuming that what they learned could to some degree apply to human behavior.

title: The cognitive revolution
description: From the 1950s, linguistics, neuroscience and computer science brought the mind back into psychology, which began modeling it as an information processor; Neisser's 1967 textbook named the field.

facts.text: By the 1950s, new work in linguistics, neuroscience and computer science revived interest in the mind as a subject of science, a shift known as the cognitive revolution.

Around 1956, computers had existed for only a few years, and pioneers were founding artificial intelligence; most cognitive science since assumes the mind has representations like computer data structures and procedures like algorithms.
In 1967, Ulric Neisser published the first textbook titled Cognitive Psychology.

title: Chomsky's challenge to behaviorism
description: In 1959 Noam Chomsky argued that behaviorism could not explain how children learn language, since they understand and produce sentences they have never heard.

facts.text: In 1959, the linguist Noam Chomsky published a review of B. F. Skinner's book on verbal behavior arguing that behaviorist models cannot explain how young children learn language so quickly.
Chomsky pointed out that by age four or five children can understand and produce sentences they have never heard, and argued that language learning does not depend on detailed reinforcement.

title: Twin and adoption studies
description: Twin studies compare identical and fraternal twins, and adoption studies compare biological and adoptive relatives, to weigh genes against environment.

facts.text: Many questions psychologists would like to answer cannot be studied with experiments because of ethical concerns.
Twin studies compare how often a trait is shared by identical twins versus fraternal twins; adoption studies compare biological relatives with adoptive relatives.

Identical twins have almost no differences in their DNA, while fraternal twins share on average 50 percent of their DNA; if a trait is more similar in identical twins raised together than in fraternal twins, genes likely play a role.

title: What heritability means
description: Heritability estimates how much of the variation in a trait within one population comes from genetic differences; twin studies put the average near half, and it says nothing about one person or how changeable a trait is.

facts.text: A 2015 analysis by Tinca Polderman and colleagues of virtually all twin studies published over 50 years, covering 17,804 traits and about 14.5 million twin pairs, found an average heritability of 49 percent across all traits.

Heritability describes how much of the variation in a trait within a population is due to genetic differences; a heritability of 0.7 does not mean a trait is 70 percent caused by genes, and an estimate applies to one population in one environment.
Language spoken runs in families but has a heritability of zero because it is not under genetic control, while hair color is highly heritable yet easy to change with dye.

title: Case studies
description: A case study examines one person or a few people in depth: rich information, but hard to generalize because the cases are usually unusual.

facts.text: A case study focuses on one person or just a few individuals, and the richness of information it gathers is unmatched by any other single research method.
Case studies often focus on people with rare characteristics, so their findings can be hard to generalize to most other people.

title: Naturalistic observation
description: Researchers watch behavior in its natural setting while staying unnoticed, because people act less naturally when they know they are watched.

facts.text: Asked in class whether they always wash their hands after using the restroom, almost everyone may raise a hand, because many people are not comfortable answering such questions honestly.

Naturalistic observation means watching behavior in its natural setting, and observers stay inconspicuous because people who know they are being watched are less likely to behave naturally, as a driver followed by a police car might.
In 1960 Jane Goodall set up camp in the Gombe Stream reserve in Tanzania and began observing wild chimpanzees, a famous example of naturalistic observation.
Naturalistic observation gives realistic data, but researchers have no control over when, or whether, the behavior they want to see will happen.

title: Surveys and self-report
description: Surveys reach many people quickly but give less depth, and self-reports can be wrong because people lie, misremember or answer to look good.

facts.text: Surveys are lists of questions that make it easy to collect data from large numbers of people, but they cannot gather the same depth of information on each person as a case study.
People do not always answer surveys accurately: they may lie, misremember or answer in a way that makes them look good, for example reporting drinking less alcohol than they do.
Case studies, observation and surveys can find relationships between things, but only an experiment can show cause and effect.

title: Informed consent and debriefing
description: Before a study, participants learn what to expect, including risks, agree voluntarily and may quit at any time; if a study used deception, they get a full debriefing.

facts.text: An informed consent form describes what participants can expect, including risks; it makes clear that taking part is voluntary and can be stopped at any time without penalty, and that data stay confidential.
When participants are under 18, their parents or legal guardians must sign the informed consent form.
When a study uses deception, participants must receive a full debriefing at the end that honestly explains the study's purpose and why deception was needed.

title: Ethics review boards
description: In the United States, an institutional review board of scientists, administrators and community members must generally approve research on people before it starts.

facts.text: In the United States, any institution that receives federal support for research with people must have an institutional review board (IRB), a committee of scientists, administrators and community members that reviews study proposals; generally, a study needs its approval to go ahead.

title: Why research ethics rules exist
description: The Nuremberg Code (1947) and the exposure of the Tuskegee syphilis study (1972) led to the US National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979).

facts.text: In 1947, the verdict in the trial of Nazi doctors who experimented on concentration camp prisoners set out ten points, known as the Nuremberg Code, starting with the rule that voluntary consent is absolutely essential.
In 1932, the US Public Health Service began a study of syphilis in 600 Black men in Alabama, 399 with the disease and 201 without, without collecting their informed consent.
The men with syphilis were never told they had it, and although penicillin became an effective treatment in the 1940s, they were not given it.
The Tuskegee study ended in 1972 after the press exposed it, and the outrage led directly to the National Research Act of 1974.
The Belmont Report of 1979, written by a commission created under the National Research Act, set out three principles for research on people: respect for persons, beneficence and justice.

title: From philosophy to science
description: Questions about the mind belonged to philosophy from Plato and Aristotle until the 19th century, when Wundt and James turned psychology into its own science.

facts.text: Attempts to understand the mind go back at least to ancient Greek philosophers such as Plato and Aristotle, and the study of mind remained part of philosophy until the nineteenth century, when experimental psychology developed.

Psychology became accepted as its own academic discipline in the late 1800s, and Wilhelm Wundt in Germany and William James in the United States are generally credited as its founders as a science separate from philosophy.
